title: Yellow eyes in a 23-year-old returned traveller
desc: This station involves a focused history and gastrointestinal examination of a 23-year-old university student whose housemates noticed his eyes were yellow, a week after nausea, chills, anorexia and right upper quadrant discomfort. He came back 4 weeks ago from South East Asia, where he ate local food, drank heavily and had unprotected sex, and he does not know his vaccination status. The candidate then interprets his liver and blood tests, hepatitis serology and STI screen, recognises acute hepatitis A with preserved liver function, and plans supportive care, public health notification, management of contacts, hepatitis B vaccination, repeat HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B and C testing after the window period, and safety netting.
focus: Approach to jaundice in a returned traveller: history of risk factors, a GI examination with few signs, LFT patterns, hepatitis serology and public health management
stem: You are a medical student on placement at a general practice. Josh, a 23-year-old university student, has come in because his eyes have turned yellow. Your supervising GP has asked you to see him first.
tasks: Take a focused history from Josh and perform a focused gastrointestinal examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Josh's blood test results, his hepatitis serology and his STI and HIV screen. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Josh, a 23-year-old university student. You feel nearly back to normal and are relaxed, but a bit embarrassed when asked about sex and drinking. If the candidate explains that what you say is confidential and asks without judging you, answer openly. Otherwise give short answers. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "My housemates reckon my eyes have gone yellow. I didn't really notice until they said something."

The illness (give only when asked):

  • Your housemates noticed your eyes 2 days ago. When you looked in the mirror the whites of your eyes looked a bit yellow. You don't think your skin is yellow.
  • Over the past week: slight nausea but no vomiting, some chills (you didn't take your temperature) and you have gone off your food. You put it down to getting back into study and work.
  • Over the same week, a continuous dull discomfort under your right ribs, about 3 out of 10. It doesn't come in waves, doesn't go anywhere else and isn't worse after fatty food.
  • For the past 4 or 5 days your wee has been darker than usual, like strong tea.
  • Most of it has settled now. Apart from your eyes you feel nearly back to normal.

Say no to all of these if asked:

  • Pale or greasy poo, diarrhoea, blood in your poo or black poo. Your bowels are normal.
  • Itching, weight loss.
  • Confusion, drowsiness, bruising easily, bleeding gums or nosebleeds.
  • Vomiting, vomiting blood.
  • High fevers, drenching sweats or shaking attacks, a rash, a sore throat or joint pains.
  • Feeling short of breath or very tired, a swollen tummy or swollen legs.

Travel (give only when asked):

  • Three weeks in Thailand and Vietnam with three friends. You got back 4 weeks ago. Cities, islands and beaches; no rural trekking.
  • You ate local street food every day, had drinks with ice and ate salads. "Lots of drinks."
  • You didn't see a doctor before you went: no travel vaccines, no malaria tablets.
  • A few mosquito bites, but no high fevers while you were away.
  • None of your friends has gone yellow, as far as you know.

Sexual history (give only when asked):

  • Several sexual encounters on the trip: three different women, vaginal and oral sex. You didn't always use condoms.
  • The last was about 5 weeks ago, near the end of the trip. No sex since you got back.
  • No discharge, burning when passing urine, sores or rash. You have never had an STI test.

Blood-borne virus risks (give only when asked): you have never injected drugs. No tattoos or piercings, here or overseas. No blood transfusions, and no medical or dental treatment overseas.

Past medical history: nothing significant. You have never been jaundiced or had liver problems.

Medications: no regular medicines. Paracetamol sometimes for hangovers: 2 tablets (1 g) the morning after a big night, about once a week. You took it once or twice last week for the chills. Never more than the packet says. No herbal remedies, supplements or gym supplements.

Allergies: none.

Vaccinations: "I'm not sure. I think I had the usual ones as a kid. Mum would know." You grew up in Australia.

Family history: no liver disease, and no one in the family has been jaundiced.

Social history:

  • You live in a share house with three housemates and share a kitchen and bathroom.
  • Full-time university student, with a casual job tutoring high school students. You don't prepare or handle food at work.
  • Alcohol, only if asked how much: 8 or more standard drinks on Friday and Saturday nights. None since you started feeling unwell.
  • Smoking: a social smoker, a few cigarettes when you are drinking.
  • No other drugs.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Ideas: "I figured it was something I ate over there, or maybe I just partied too hard."
  • Concern, only if the candidate has taken a sexual history or asks what is worrying you: "Could it be something like HIV?"
  • Expectation: you want to know what it is, whether you need tests, and to get back to uni.

Question to raise once in Part 1: "Is it something I caught overseas?"

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General inspection: well and alert, no distress. Normal build (weight 74 kg, height 180 cm, BMI 23). Not oedematous.
  • Vital signs: BP 124/81, HR 71 regular, RR 12, temperature 37.4 °C, SpO2 98% on room air.
  • Hands: no clubbing, leukonychia, palmar erythema or Dupuytren's contracture. No flap (asterixis).
  • Arms: no bruising, petechiae or muscle wasting.
  • Eyes: mild scleral icterus. No conjunctival pallor.
  • Mouth: normal. No ulcers, normal tongue.
  • Neck, chest and back: no cervical, supraclavicular or axillary lymphadenopathy. No spider naevi. No gynaecomastia.
  • Abdomen, inspection: not distended. No scars, masses, visible pulsation, spider naevi, caput medusae or hernias.
  • Abdomen, palpation: soft and non-tender with no guarding in all 9 regions, on light and deep palpation. Liver edge not palpable. Spleen and kidneys not palpable. Aorta normal.
  • Percussion: liver span about 10 cm. No shifting dullness (no ascites).
  • Auscultation: normal bowel sounds. No renal bruits.
  • Special tests: Murphy's sign negative. No tenderness at McBurney's point; Rovsing's sign negative. No peritonism (no guarding, rebound or percussion tenderness).
  • Legs: no oedema.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms Josh's identity, and explains and gains consent for the history and examination.
Explains confidentiality before the sexual, alcohol and drug history, asks without judging him, and uses plain language throughout.
History
Characterises the jaundice and the illness before it:

kids.x: Onset: housemates noticed his yellow eyes 2 days ago; skin not noticeably yellow.
Prodrome over the past week: slight nausea without vomiting, chills and reduced appetite, now largely settled.
Right upper quadrant discomfort: continuous and dull under the right ribs, not colicky, no radiation, not linked to fatty food.

check.x: Asks the questions that separate pre-hepatic, hepatic and post-hepatic jaundice: urine colour (dark for a few days, which means conjugated bilirubin and is against a pre-hepatic cause), stool colour (normal), itch and weight loss (absent).
Screens for features of liver failure and haemolysis: confusion or drowsiness, bruising or bleeding, persistent vomiting, and tiredness or breathlessness (all absent).
check.d: Award for at least three of these.

check.x: Takes a travel history:

kids.x: Where, when and how long: Thailand and Vietnam for 3 weeks, back 4 weeks ago.
Exposures and preparation: local street food, ice and salads; no pre-travel consultation, travel vaccines or malaria tablets; mosquito bites without high fevers.
kids.d: Award for food and water exposure plus either pre-travel preparation or mosquito exposure.

check.x: Takes a sexual and blood-borne virus risk history:

kids.x: Number and gender of partners, type of sex, condom use and timing: three women on the trip, condoms not always used, last about 5 weeks ago, none since.
Injecting drug use, tattoos or piercings, transfusions and medical or dental treatment overseas (none), and STI symptoms (none).

check.x: Takes a medication history that quantifies paracetamol (1 g after a big night, about once a week, and once or twice last week), and asks about herbal or other supplements (none) and allergies (none).
check.d: The paracetamol dose and frequency must be quantified, not just noted.

check.x: Quantifies alcohol (8 or more standard drinks on Friday and Saturday nights, none since unwell), and asks about smoking (social) and other drugs (none).

Asks about vaccination status (unsure), past medical history (nil, no previous jaundice), family history of liver disease (none) and social situation: share house with three housemates, university student, casual tutor who does not handle food.
check.d: Award for vaccination status plus his household and occupation (who could be exposed, and whether he is a food handler).

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it was food or partying, worried it could be HIV, wants to know what it is and get back to uni.
Examination
Positions him lying flat and exposes the abdomen to the pubic symphysis while keeping him covered, and checks he is comfortable.
Asks for the vital signs and notes a temperature of 37.4 °C with otherwise normal observations; on general inspection notes he is well, of normal build and not oedematous.
Looks for peripheral signs of chronic liver disease:

kids.x: Hands: clubbing, leukonychia, palmar erythema, Dupuytren's contracture, and asterixis (flap).
Arms, neck, chest and back: bruising, petechiae, wasting, lymph nodes, spider naevi and gynaecomastia.

check.x: Inspects the sclerae in natural light and identifies mild scleral icterus, and checks the conjunctivae for pallor.
Examines the abdomen:

kids.x: Palpates all 9 regions, light then deep, watching his face: soft and non-tender with no guarding.
Palpates for the liver from the right iliac fossa upwards and percusses the liver span (about 10 cm, not enlarged); palpates for the spleen from the right iliac fossa and ballots the kidneys.
Inspects for distension, scars, caput medusae and hernias, percusses for ascites, and listens for bowel sounds and renal bruits.

check.x: Performs Murphy's sign and checks for peritonism (negative).

Completes the examination (checks the legs for oedema, thanks him and offers help to dress) and summarises: a well young man with mild scleral icterus, a temperature of 37.4 °C, no signs of chronic liver disease and no hepatosplenomegaly.
check.d: Award if the candidate says they would complete these steps, without needing time to do them.

check.x: Interpretation

Reads the liver tests as a hepatocellular pattern: ALT 1,240 and AST 610 far more raised than the ALP (162) and GGT (148), ALT higher than AST, with a mainly conjugated bilirubin (46, conjugated 34). This is hepatic jaundice, not obstruction; normal haemoglobin and lipase are against haemolysis and pancreatitis.
States that liver synthetic function is preserved: INR 1.1 and albumin 41 are normal, so there is no sign of acute liver failure; creatinine is normal.
Reads hepatitis A IgM detected as acute hepatitis A infection.

Reads the other serology: HBsAg and anti-HBc negative with anti-HBs 3 means no hepatitis B infection and no serological evidence of immunity (protected only if a primary course is documented); hepatitis C antibody and hepatitis E IgM negative.

States that the HIV and syphilis (and hepatitis B and C) blood tests were taken only about 5 weeks after his last exposure, inside their window periods, so they need repeating at about 3 months; the chlamydia and gonorrhoea urine NAATs are outside their ~2-week window, so the negatives are reliable.

Gives acute hepatitis A (hepatic jaundice; prodrome settling, early in the jaundiced phase) as the most likely diagnosis and justifies it: prodrome then jaundice after eating local food in an endemic area, few signs, a hepatocellular pattern and a positive hepatitis A IgM.
Gives differentials, each with a feature for or against:
check.d: Also credit other reasonable differentials (e.g. hepatitis E, EBV or CMV hepatitis, malaria or dengue in a returned traveller) given with a feature for or against.

kids.x: Acute hepatitis B: unprotected sex overseas; against: HBsAg and anti-HBc negative.

Drug- or alcohol-related liver injury: paracetamol for hangovers and binge drinking; against: paracetamol: only occasional standard doses and a normal INR; alcohol: ALT higher than AST and over 1,000.

Post-hepatic obstruction (for example a bile duct stone) or a pre-hepatic cause (haemolysis or Gilbert's syndrome); against: hepatocellular pattern, normal-coloured stools and no itch, conjugated bilirubin with dark urine (against pre-hepatic), and a normal haemoglobin.
kids.d: Award for either, with a feature against.

check.x: Management

Explains in plain words that this is hepatitis A, which settles by itself, does not become long-term, and is not caused by HIV. Plans supportive care at home (rest, fluids, small meals, no specific antiviral), stating that he does not need hospital because he is well with a normal INR.

Protects the liver: no alcohol at all (including at his friend's 21st) until his liver tests are back to normal, paracetamol only at the recommended dose and not for hangovers, and no herbal remedies or supplements.
check.d: Credit the answer to his question about drinking at his friend's 21st here.

check.x: Gives brief alcohol advice for later: no more than 4 standard drinks on any day and 10 a week (NHMRC); his weekend drinking is above this. Offers support.
check.d: Credit whether given here or in the safety-netting answer.

check.x: Advises how to stop the spread:

kids.x: Careful handwashing after the toilet and before eating, not preparing food for others, and not sharing towels, utensils or drinks.
Stays home from university and tutoring, and avoids sex, until at least 1 week after his eyes turned yellow.

check.x: Ensures hepatitis A is notified and phones the local public health unit, because it is notifiable and contact management is needed.

His housemates are offered hepatitis A vaccine as post-exposure prophylaxis via public health (ideally within 2 weeks, still offered as exposure is ongoing) and told the symptoms to watch for; travel companions told to see their GP if unwell.
check.d: The housemates have been exposed for about 3 weeks, since Josh became infectious about 2 weeks before his prodrome, so they could already be incubating; vaccine is still offered because exposure is ongoing, and they should see their GP if symptoms develop.

check.x: Offers hepatitis B vaccination (checks the Australian Immunisation Register; a course if he has no record of one).
Safety netting

Tells him to go to the ED (or call 000 if he cannot get there safely) if he becomes confused or very drowsy, bruises or bleeds easily, vomits and cannot keep fluids down, or gets severe tummy pain or a high fever; and if he becomes much more yellow, to see the GP the same day, and go to the ED if this comes with confusion, drowsiness, bleeding or vomiting.
check.d: Award for at least three red flags in plain words, linked to the ED or 000.

check.x: Arranges GP review with repeat liver tests and INR in about 1 week, then until they are normal, and offers a certificate for uni and work.
Arranges repeat HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B and C testing about 3 months after his last exposure, advises condoms with new partners, and asks him to return sooner if he gets STI symptoms.

part2.lead: Josh had blood tests and an STI screen at the end of the first consultation. The laboratory phoned the liver results through the next morning. Two days later all the results are back, and he has returned to discuss them. Here they are.
part2.patient:
Ask these once each while the candidate explains the plan:

  • "So it wasn't from the sex? It's not HIV?"
  • "Do my housemates need to do anything? Can they catch it?"
  • "My mate's 21st is next Saturday. Can I still have a few drinks?"

You are relieved the HIV test is negative so far, and accept that it needs repeating. You are a bit disappointed about the party. If the candidate uses jargon such as "hepatocellular", "serology" or "window period" without explaining it, ask what it means.

handover.label: Blood tests
handover.result: Collected at the practice at the first consultation. Liver function results phoned to the practice the next morning.
handover.model:
• Read: ALT 1,240 and AST 610, more than 15 times the upper limit, with ALT higher than AST. ALP 162 and GGT 148 only mildly raised. Bilirubin 46, mostly conjugated (34). Albumin 41 and INR 1.1 normal. Haemoglobin, white cells and platelets normal. CRP mildly raised at 9. Lipase, electrolytes and creatinine normal.
  • For Josh: a hepatocellular (hepatitic) pattern: the transaminases are far more raised than the ALP, which means hepatic jaundice, typical of acute viral hepatitis. An ALT over 1,000 is unusual in alcohol-related injury, where AST is usually higher than ALT. The normal haemoglobin argues against haemolysis. The modest ALP and normal stools argue against obstruction. The normal lipase argues against pancreatitis.
  • What it changes: the normal INR and albumin, and no confusion, mean liver function is preserved with no sign of acute liver failure, so he can be managed at home. The INR is the key value to repeat with the liver tests in about a week. An ultrasound is not needed with this pattern unless it becomes obstructive or he does not improve.

handover.label: Hepatitis serology
handover.result: Collected at the practice at the first consultation. Laboratory comment: hepatitis A IgM detected, consistent with acute hepatitis A infection. Hepatitis A is a notifiable condition. No serological evidence of current or past hepatitis B infection, and anti-HBs below the protective level.
handover.model:
• Read: hepatitis A IgM and total antibody detected. HBsAg and anti-HBc negative, anti-HBs 3 mIU/mL (below 10). Hepatitis C antibody not detected. Hepatitis E IgM not detected.
  • For Josh: acute hepatitis A, which fits the timing: exposure to food and water on the trip 4 to 7 weeks ago, then a prodrome and jaundice within the 15 to 50 day incubation period. No evidence of current or past hepatitis B infection. Anti-HBs below 10 mIU/mL means no serological evidence of immunity. If the Australian Immunisation Register shows a completed infant course, he is considered protected by immune memory and needs no further doses; if there is no record, he is presumed susceptible and needs a full course. No hepatitis C or E.
  • What it changes: hepatitis A is self-limiting and does not become chronic, so he needs supportive care, not antivirals. It is notifiable, and he is infectious now, so public health is involved for his housemates' post-exposure vaccination. He will be immune to hepatitis A for life, so needs no hepatitis A vaccine. Check the Australian Immunisation Register for hepatitis B vaccination and give a course if there is no documented primary course.

rows.n: acute or past infection, or vaccination

handover.label: HIV and STI screen
handover.result: Blood and first-pass urine collected at the practice at the first consultation. Clinical details: unprotected heterosexual contact overseas; last exposure about 5 weeks before collection.
handover.model:
• Read: HIV antigen and antibody, syphilis antibody, and chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT on first-pass urine are all not detected.
  • For Josh: reassuring, and it answers his worry for now, but the blood tests were taken about 5 weeks after his last exposure, inside the window periods for HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B and C (the hepatitis C antibody is in the hepatitis serology), so they cannot exclude infection yet. The urine NAATs are outside their window of about 2 weeks, so those negatives are reliable. Post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV is no longer possible, as it must start within 72 hours.
  • What it changes: repeat HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B and C testing about 3 months after the last exposure. Advise condoms with any new partner, offer hepatitis B vaccination if he has no documented course, and tell him to return sooner with STI symptoms.

ask: You are now handing Josh over to your supervising GP. Please give an ISBAR handover of Josh, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Josh now, here in general practice.
Before Josh goes home, what would you tell him and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student at the practice; Josh, 23, university student.
  • Situation: jaundice; results show acute hepatitis A with liver function preserved.
  • Background: One week of nausea, chills, anorexia, RUQ discomfort and dark urine, now settling; yellow eyes 2 days. Back 4 weeks from Thailand/Vietnam: street food, unprotected sex, no travel vaccines. Exam: mild icterus, 37.4 °C, otherwise normal.
  • Assessment: ALT 1,240, AST 610, conjugated bilirubin: hepatocellular. INR 1.1, albumin 41: no liver failure. HAV IgM positive. No hepatitis B infection, anti-HBs below 10 (no serological immunity); HCV and HEV negative. HIV and syphilis negative but within the window period; chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAATs reliably negative.
  • Recommendation: Home care, notify public health for housemates' PEP, hepatitis B vaccine if no documented course, LFTs/INR in 1 week, retest at 3 months.

Most likely: acute hepatitis A, hepatic jaundice, prodrome settling. Supporting: prodrome (nausea, chills, anorexia, right upper quadrant discomfort) then jaundice, 4 to 7 weeks after local food and drink in an endemic area, no travel vaccines, few signs, hepatocellular LFTs, HAV IgM positive.

  • Acute hepatitis B: unprotected sex; against: HBsAg and anti-HBc negative.
  • Hepatitis E: enteric spread in Asia; against: HEV IgM negative.
  • Paracetamol or alcohol liver injury: hangover paracetamol, binge drinking; against: paracetamol only occasional standard doses with a normal INR; alcohol: ALT higher than AST and over 1,000.
  • Post-hepatic obstruction: right upper quadrant discomfort; against: hepatocellular pattern, normal-coloured stools, no itch, Murphy's negative.
  • Pre-hepatic (haemolysis, Gilbert's): against: conjugated bilirubin, raised ALT, normal haemoglobin.

1. Explain in plain words: hepatitis A, most likely caught from food or water on the trip; hepatitis A can also spread during sex, which is why he should avoid sex until 1 week after the jaundice began. It settles by itself, does not become long-term, and gives lifelong immunity. The jaundice is not caused by HIV; the first HIV test is negative but needs repeating at 3 months to be sure.
  2. Supportive care at home: rest, fluids, small meals, no antiviral. No hospital needed: well, INR normal.
  3. Protect the liver: no alcohol until LFTs normal, paracetamol only at the recommended dose, no supplements.
  4. Stop spread: handwashing, don't prepare food for others or share towels or utensils. Stay home from uni and tutoring, and avoid sex, until at least 1 week after jaundice began.
  5. Public health: notifiable; phone the public health unit. Housemates offered hepatitis A vaccine via public health (ideally within 2 weeks of exposure; still offered as exposure is ongoing) and told the symptoms to watch for; tell travel companions to see their GP if unwell.
  6. Hepatitis B vaccination: check the Immunisation Register; a course if no documented primary course.

• Go to the ED (or call 000) if he becomes confused or very drowsy, bruises or bleeds easily, vomits and cannot keep fluids down, or has severe tummy pain or a high fever.
  • If he becomes much more yellow: see the GP the same day; go to the ED if this comes with confusion, drowsiness, bleeding or vomiting.
  • Drinking: no alcohol at the 21st, or at all, until his liver tests are normal; then keep to no more than 4 standard drinks on any day.
  • Follow-up: GP review with repeat LFTs and INR in about 1 week, then until normal; medical certificate.
  • Retesting: HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B and C about 3 months after his last exposure; condoms with new partners; return sooner with discharge, burning, sores or a rash.
  • Written information on hepatitis A and safe sex.

ddx.for: Prodrome of nausea, chills, anorexia and right upper quadrant discomfort then jaundice, 4 to 7 weeks after eating street food in Thailand and Vietnam with no travel vaccines, with hepatocellular LFTs and a positive hepatitis A IgM.
Unprotected sex with three partners overseas about 5 weeks ago, and an uncertain vaccination history.
ddx.against: HBsAg and anti-HBc are both negative.

ddx.for: Enterically transmitted hepatitis after local food and water in Asia.
ddx.against: Hepatitis E IgM not detected, and hepatitis A IgM is positive.

ddx.dx: Paracetamol or other drug-induced liver injury
ddx.for: Takes paracetamol for hangovers and took it last week while unwell.
ddx.against: Only occasional doses within the recommended amount, a normal INR, and a positive hepatitis A IgM.

ddx.for: Binge drinks 8 or more standard drinks on weekend nights.
ddx.against: ALT higher than AST and above 1,000, no signs of chronic liver disease, and no alcohol since he became unwell.

ddx.dx: Post-hepatic (obstructive) jaundice from a common bile duct stone
ddx.for: Jaundice with right upper quadrant discomfort.
ddx.against: Pain not colicky, normal-coloured stools, no itch, Murphy's sign negative, and a hepatocellular rather than cholestatic pattern.

guide:
This is a general practice station, so there is no observation chart. Give the vital signs from the Exam findings when the candidate asks for them. In Part 1, the examiner gives findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. The examination is normal apart from mild scleral icterus and a temperature of 37.4 °C. If the candidate asks for tests in Part 1, say the results will be given in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over all three results, then ask the four questions in order. Josh asks his three questions once each while the candidate explains the plan.

This station assesses the examination, so give the examination marks fully. Credit a candidate who says they would complete steps (legs, helping him dress) without doing them. Most peripheral signs of liver disease reflect chronic disease, so their absence is expected and should be stated, not invented.

A high-performing candidate takes a risk-factor history for jaundice: travel, food and water, sexual partners and condom use, injecting drugs and tattoos, quantified paracetamol and alcohol, and vaccination. They take the sexual history sensitively and pick up his worry about HIV. They examine the eyes and abdomen systematically and percuss the liver span. In Part 2 they read the hepatocellular pattern and the preserved INR, diagnose acute hepatitis A, see that the hepatitis B result means not infected and no serological immunity and check the Immunisation Register, and know the HIV and syphilis blood tests are within the window period. They notify public health, arrange post-exposure vaccination for the housemates, offer hepatitis B vaccine, ban alcohol for now, and give clear liver failure red flags.

A borderline candidate takes a generic abdominal history and misses the sexual or travel history. They may read the negative HIV test as final, miss the notification and contacts, read the hepatitis B result as immune, send him to hospital without reason, or allow him to drink at the party.
explain:
Diagnosis

Josh has acute hepatitis A, a hepatic (hepatocellular) jaundice in its early jaundiced phase. The story is typical. A prodrome of nausea, chills, anorexia and right upper quadrant discomfort, then dark urine, was followed by jaundice, 4 to 7 weeks after eating street food and drinking iced drinks in an endemic area with no travel vaccines. That fits the incubation period of 15 to 50 days (about 28 days on average). The prodrome often settles as jaundice appears, which is why he feels nearly well. A single set of results gives no trend; repeat LFTs and INR show whether it is improving. By the time patients present, acute viral hepatitis often has few or no signs beyond icterus.

Approach to jaundice

  • Pre-hepatic: haemolysis or Gilbert's syndrome. The bilirubin is unconjugated, the urine is normal, and with haemolysis there is anaemia.
  • Hepatic: viral hepatitis, drugs (including paracetamol), alcohol, autoimmune and metabolic disease. The transaminases are much higher than the ALP. The bilirubin is largely conjugated, so the urine is often dark.
  • Post-hepatic (obstructive): stones, strictures or tumours, with dark urine, pale stools and itch, and the ALP and GGT raised more than the transaminases. An ultrasound looks for duct dilatation. Dark urine occurs in both hepatic and post-hepatic jaundice; pale stools and itch are what point to obstruction.

Painless obstructive jaundice in an older person is pancreatic or biliary cancer until proven otherwise. Josh's jaundice followed a painful prodrome in a young man.

The examination

Most peripheral signs of gastrointestinal disease (leukonychia, clubbing, palmar erythema, Dupuytren's contracture, spider naevi, gynaecomastia, caput medusae, ascites) reflect chronic liver disease, so they are absent in an acute illness. Their absence is a useful finding. Asterixis and confusion would suggest encephalopathy and acute liver failure. If the abdomen is distended, think of the causes: fat, fluid, flatus, faeces, fetus, and fluid-filled or solid masses.

Interpreting the results

  • Liver tests: ALT 1,240 and AST 610 with a modest ALP and GGT is a hepatocellular pattern. Transaminases over 1,000 point to viral, toxic (paracetamol) or ischaemic hepatitis rather than alcohol, where AST is usually higher than ALT and rarely above a few hundred. The bilirubin is mostly conjugated.
  • Synthetic function: the INR is the best marker of how sick the liver is in acute hepatitis. A normal INR and albumin, with no encephalopathy, mean he can be managed at home. A rising INR, confusion or hypoglycaemia mean acute liver failure and need urgent hospital and liver unit referral.
  • FBC, lipase, UEC and CRP: a normal haemoglobin argues against haemolysis, a normal lipase against pancreatitis, normal renal function is reassuring, and a mildly raised CRP fits a viral illness.
  • Hepatitis serology: hepatitis A IgM means acute infection. HBsAg and anti-HBc negative with anti-HBs below 10 mIU/mL means no hepatitis B infection and no serological evidence of immunity. If he has a documented primary course (likely, as universal infant vaccination began in Australia in 2000), he is considered protected by immune memory despite the low antibody level. Hepatitis C antibody and hepatitis E IgM are negative.
  • HIV and STI screen: negative, but the blood tests were taken about 5 weeks after his last exposure, inside the window periods for HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B, so testing is repeated about 3 months after exposure. The urine NAATs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea are outside their window of about 2 weeks, so those negatives are reliable.

Initial investigations for jaundice in primary care: FBC, CRP, LFTs, lipase, UEC, INR, hepatitis A, B, C (and E) serology, and HIV and STI testing with consent.

Differentials that matter

  • Acute hepatitis B: unprotected sex overseas makes it a must-exclude; excluded by negative HBsAg and anti-HBc. It can take months to appear, which is another reason to retest.
  • Hepatitis E: spread the same way as hepatitis A, and common in parts of Asia.
  • Paracetamol or drug-induced liver injury: always quantify paracetamol, including the "hangover" doses, and ask about supplements.
  • Alcohol-related liver injury: his binge drinking is relevant, but the pattern does not fit.
  • EBV or CMV hepatitis: considered in young adults, especially with a sore throat or lymphadenopathy.
  • Febrile returned traveller: malaria, dengue and leptospirosis can cause fever with jaundice. They are considered according to the itinerary and the fever, and investigated urgently if suspected. His itinerary (cities, islands, beaches, no rural or forest travel) carries negligible malaria risk and he has had no measured fever, but credit a candidate who requests malaria films or a rapid antigen test. Dengue is excluded by timing (incubation up to 14 days; his illness began about 3 weeks after return).

Management

  • Supportive care: there is no specific antiviral treatment. Rest, fluids and nutrition. Avoid alcohol until the liver tests are normal, use paracetamol only at recommended doses, and avoid herbal remedies and supplements. Hepatitis A does not cause chronic infection, and infection gives lifelong immunity.
  • Infection control: hepatitis A spreads by the faecal-oral route. People are most infectious from about 2 weeks before symptoms until about 1 week after jaundice starts. Advise careful handwashing, no preparing food for others, no sharing of towels or utensils, and avoiding sex during this time. National guidance excludes food handlers, childcare workers and healthcare workers from work until 1 week after the onset of jaundice. Josh is not in these groups, but he should stay home from university and tutoring for the same period.
  • Public health: hepatitis A is notifiable in every Australian state and territory. The laboratory notifies, and the GP should contact the public health unit promptly so contacts can be managed.
  • Contacts: the Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends post-exposure prophylaxis for household and sexual contacts, ideally within 2 weeks of exposure. This is hepatitis A vaccine for most people, and normal human immunoglobulin for some (for example people who are immunocompromised or have chronic liver disease). His housemates share a kitchen and bathroom and qualify. Josh became infectious about 2 weeks before his prodrome, so his housemates have been exposed for about 3 weeks and could already be incubating. Post-exposure vaccine is still offered because exposure is ongoing, but housemates should also be told the symptoms and to see their GP if they develop them. His travel companions shared the original exposure and should see their GP if they become unwell.
  • Vaccination and prevention: his anti-HBs is below 10 mIU/mL, so there is no serological evidence of immunity to hepatitis B. Check the Australian Immunisation Register: if it shows a completed primary course, he is considered protected by immune memory and needs no further doses; if there is no record, he is presumed susceptible and needs a full course. He needs no hepatitis A vaccine. Advise condoms with new partners and a pre-travel consultation before future trips.
  • Alcohol and smoking: 8 or more standard drinks on a night is above the NHMRC guideline of no more than 10 a week and no more than 4 on any one day. Give brief advice and offer support.

Safety netting and follow-up

He should go to the ED (or call 000 if he cannot get there safely) if he becomes confused or drowsy, bruises or bleeds, cannot keep fluids down, or has severe abdominal pain or a high fever. These can signal acute liver failure, which is rare in hepatitis A. If he becomes much more jaundiced, he should see the GP the same day, and go to the ED if this comes with confusion, drowsiness, bleeding or vomiting. Repeat the liver tests and INR in about a week and until they are normal. Repeat HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B and C testing about 3 months after his last exposure, and complete the hepatitis B vaccine course if one was started.
points: Classify jaundice as pre-hepatic, hepatic or post-hepatic using the urine and stool colour, itch, and the LFT pattern (transaminases versus ALP and GGT, conjugated versus unconjugated bilirubin).
The jaundice history needs specific risk factors: travel and food, sexual partners and condom use, injecting drugs and tattoos, quantified paracetamol and alcohol, and vaccination status.
Acute viral hepatitis often has few signs. Peripheral GI signs mostly reflect chronic liver disease and are expected to be absent; the INR and mental state show whether the liver is failing.

Hepatitis A IgM confirms acute hepatitis A, which is self-limiting, never chronic and notifiable. Household and sexual contacts are offered post-exposure hepatitis A vaccine, ideally within 2 weeks of exposure.
HBsAg and anti-HBc negative with anti-HBs below 10 mIU/mL means not infected and no serological immunity: check the Immunisation Register and give a course if there is no documented primary course.

Negative HIV, syphilis and hepatitis serology taken within the window period after an exposure must be repeated, at about 3 months; urine NAATs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea are reliable from about 2 weeks.
